headline: Astronomers Discover Youngest Planet Ever—Less Than a Million Years Old
meta_description: Elias 2-24 b, a Jupiter-size world less than 1 million years old, challenges everything scientists thought they knew about how giant planets form.
summary_short: Astronomers have confirmed a Jupiter-size planet still being born, less than a million years old. The discovery challenges leading theories about planetary formation.
body:
Astronomers have confirmed a Jupiter-size planet less than 1 million years old, making Elias 2-24 b the youngest known world ever observed and offering scientists an unprecedented window into how planets actually form. Located 450 light-years from Earth, the planet still orbits within its young star's dusty disk—the very material from which it is still being born. This discovery, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters on September 16, reshapes our understanding of planetary birth, because current models predicted that forming a giant planet at such a great distance from its star should take far longer than what appears to have happened here.

The breakthrough came from detective work spanning a decade. Earlier observations had revealed a mysterious gap in the dust surrounding the star Elias 2-24, and a faint point of light within it. Scientists debated for years whether this object could actually be a forming planet, since existing theory suggested it shouldn't be possible. Andrea Bernardi, a doctoral candidate at the Universidad Diego Portales in Chile, and her team searched archived observations from the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii collected in 2018 and 2020. By tracking how the object moved over time across multiple observations, they confirmed it was indeed a planet orbiting the star—not an imaging artifact or distant background object.

The implications are profound. "Our planet-formation models already struggled to explain" the previous youngest planets, said co-author Lucas Cieza. "Elias 2-24 b shows us that even our best models are still missing some important processes." Because thick dust typically hides forming planets, astronomers remain largely blind to how planetary birth actually unfolds. This discovery suggests that future telescopes, including NASA's upcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, will reveal many more baby planets and force scientists to rethink how worlds take shape.
quick_facts: Jupiter-size planet less than 1 million years old
Located 450 light-years from Earth, still surrounded by birth dust
Confirmed using archived W.M. Keck Observatory data from 2018-2020
Challenges theories predicting giant planets take 5+ million years to form
